concepts.title: Goroutines: Lightweight Concurrent Functions
concepts.description: A goroutine is a function that runs concurrently with the rest of your program, scheduled by the Go runtime rather than the operating system. This concept covers why goroutines are cheap, why the main goroutine exiting kills the rest, and how they leak.
learningObjectives: Launch a goroutine with the `go` keyword and explain what actually happens when you do.
Explain why goroutines are described as 'lightweight' compared to OS threads, in concrete terms (stack size, scheduling).
Predict what happens to running goroutines when the main function returns.
Explain why a loop variable captured by a goroutine closure can produce surprising results, and how Go 1.22+ changed that.
Identify a goroutine leak: a goroutine that will never terminate because nothing will ever unblock it.

sections.heading: Starting a Goroutine
Concurrency vs. Parallelism, and What a Goroutine Costs
sections.body:
Two words that are easy to blur: **concurrency is about structuring a program as multiple independently-progressing activities; parallelism is about running more than one of them at the same instant, on separate CPU cores.** A single-core machine can absolutely run a highly concurrent Go program (dozens of goroutines, each making progress in small interleaved slices of time) without ever executing two of them in parallel; the runtime is switching between them fast enough that they *appear* to make simultaneous progress. Parallelism needs multiple cores executing separate goroutines at the same moment. 'Concurrency is not parallelism,' as the title of a well-known talk by Rob Pike (one of Go's creators) puts it. You express the concurrent structure with goroutines and channels, and the runtime decides how much of it runs in parallel, based on `GOMAXPROCS` and the cores available.

Goroutines are managed by the Go runtime's own scheduler, not by the operating system. The OS has no idea individual goroutines exist at all; it only sees a handful of OS threads that the Go runtime multiplexes many goroutines onto. This is what people mean when they call goroutines 'lightweight'. An OS thread typically reserves address space for a large stack when it's created (1MB by default on Windows, commonly 8MB on Linux), and creating or switching threads goes through the OS kernel. A goroutine starts with a tiny stack, around 2KB, that the Go runtime grows and shrinks dynamically as needed, by copying it to a larger allocation when it would otherwise overflow. The practical consequence: spinning up thousands, or even hundreds of thousands, of goroutines is routine and cheap in Go, where that many OS threads would hit memory or OS limits. That is why a Go server can afford one goroutine per connection.

The Go runtime scheduler maps many goroutines onto a much smaller number of OS threads. At most `GOMAXPROCS` of them run Go code at once (the default is the number of logical CPUs; since Go 1.25 it also respects a container's CPU limit on Linux). It switches when a goroutine blocks, for example on a channel operation, and since Go 1.14 it can also preempt a goroutine stuck in a tight loop. This is often called an M:N scheduler (M goroutines onto N OS threads). When `GOMAXPROCS` is greater than 1 and more than one goroutine is simultaneously runnable, the scheduler runs them in parallel across separate cores; when it's 1, or only one goroutine is runnable at a time, you get interleaved progress without parallelism. Your program's correctness should never depend on which of those two situations it is in.

Closures Over Loop Variables: An Old Trap, and Go 1.22's Fix
Goroutine Leaks: Goroutines That Never End

examples.title: main Returning Before a Goroutine Gets to Run
examples.explanation: As written, this program almost always prints only "main returning now". The anonymous goroutine is scheduled, but `main` typically reaches its own end and the whole process exits before the goroutine ever gets a turn to run at all. Uncommenting the `time.Sleep` line would very likely make the goroutine's print show up too, but that's not a fix. It's papering over the underlying issue by guessing at a delay long enough to usually work on your machine, in your test environment, under your current load. A slower machine, a busier CI runner, or a slightly heavier goroutine body could make even a 100ms sleep insufficient. The correct fix, shown in this module's sync.WaitGroup concept, replaces the guess with a synchronization signal that waits as long as necessary (no more, no less) regardless of timing.

examples.title: The Loop-Variable-Capture Fix for Pre-1.22 Code
examples.explanation: Each goroutine's function literal declares its own parameter, also named `i` for clarity, and the call `(i)` at the very end passes the loop's current value of `i` as an argument at the exact moment that specific goroutine is launched, before the loop moves on to the next iteration. This gives every goroutine its own independent copy of the value, sidestepping the historical shared-variable trap, regardless of Go version. On Go 1.22+, this explicit parameter-passing is no longer strictly necessary. The loop variable itself is now scoped per-iteration by the language, but writing it this way remains completely correct and, arguably, still a clearer signal of intent to a reader who doesn't have the exact Go version memorized. sync.WaitGroup here (covered in depth later in this module) is what makes wg.Wait() block until all three goroutines have called wg.Done(), guaranteeing all three prints happen before the program exits. Without it, this would have the same 'main exits before goroutines run' problem as the previous example.

examples.title: A Goroutine Leak From an Unbuffered Channel With No Receiver
examples.explanation: When `fetchWithTimeout(true)` is called, it starts a goroutine that will eventually try to send `42` on `ch`, but the function itself takes the early-return path and returns an error *without ever executing* `<-ch`. `ch` is unbuffered, so the goroutine's send blocks until something receives, and nothing ever will, since the function that owned `ch` has already returned and nothing else has a reference to that channel. That goroutine is now parked forever, for the entire remaining lifetime of the program: not crashed, not cleaned up by the garbage collector, just leaked. Call this function from many requests in a long-running server and you accumulate one leaked, permanently-blocked goroutine per failing call: a slow, silent memory and resource leak. A fix needs the goroutine to have some way to give up too, typically via a buffered channel sized to hold one result (so the send never blocks even with no reader) or a `select` combined with a `context.Context` that gets cancelled, so the goroutine can bail out instead of blocking forever.

misconceptions.description: Calling `go someFunction()` runs someFunction() in the background but Go automatically makes sure it finishes before the program exits, similar to how a browser might finish an in-flight network request before closing a tab.
misconceptions.clarification: Go makes no such guarantee at all. The moment `main()` returns, the entire process terminates immediately, and any goroutines still running (no matter how close they were to finishing) are cut off mid-execution, with no cleanup, no completion, and no notification. There is nothing implicit protecting a goroutine's completion; if you need main to wait for a goroutine, you must say so explicitly, most commonly with a `sync.WaitGroup`, a channel receive, or another explicit synchronization mechanism: silence on your part means 'don't wait,' not 'wait as needed.'

misconceptions.description: Goroutines that are stuck waiting forever (leaked) will eventually get cleaned up by Go's garbage collector, the same way an unused object with no references does.
misconceptions.clarification: The garbage collector reclaims memory for objects that are no longer reachable by anything, but a leaked goroutine blocked on a channel operation still exists from the runtime's point of view: it is parked in a waiting state until an event (a send, a receive, an unlock) that will never occur. The collector treats its stack as a root, so anything the goroutine references stays reachable too, for the rest of the program's life. That is why leaks add up in long-running services.

exercises.prompt: What is most likely to happen when this program runs, and why is the outcome not fully guaranteed by the code itself?
hints: Think about what main() waits for after starting the 5 goroutines: is there any synchronization here at all?
The `go` keyword returns control to the next line immediately. It does not pause main to let the goroutine run first.
Without a WaitGroup, channel, or any other synchronization, there's no guarantee any of the 5 goroutines get a chance to run before main returns and the process exits.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Most likely, the program prints only "main done", with none or only some of the 5 goroutine prints appearing, and in no guaranteed order even if some do appear. This is because main() has no synchronization forcing it to wait for the goroutines, so it typically reaches its end and the process exits before the scheduler gives any of them a turn to run.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Each `go fmt.Println(...)` call starts a new goroutine and immediately returns control to the loop, without waiting for that goroutine to execute. After the loop finishes launching all 5, `main` immediately prints "main done" and returns, and the instant main returns, the entire program exits, taking any still-pending goroutines down with it before they necessarily get a chance to run. In practice you might occasionally see one or two of the numbered prints sneak in, purely due to scheduling timing, but there is no guarantee of that, and no guarantee of any particular order among the ones that do print. This unpredictability is the reason explicit synchronization (a sync.WaitGroup, covered later in this module) is needed whenever you need to wait for goroutines to finish.

exercises.prompt: This function is supposed to leave a running background goroutine that periodically sends heartbeat values on `ch`, but the goroutine blocks on its very first send until somebody reads, so it makes no progress while main sleeps, and a caller that never reads would leak it. Find and fix the bug. (Assume the caller only wants to read a heartbeat occasionally, without the sender getting stuck in between.)
hints: `ch` is created with `make(chan int)`: an unbuffered channel. What does an unbuffered send require in order to complete?

Between starting the heartbeat and the first `<-ch` read, main is doing other things (sleeping) and not reading. What is the background goroutine doing on its very first `ch <- count` during that time?

A buffered channel lets a send complete without a reader present, up to the buffer's capacity: consider giving `ch` a small buffer so the sender never has to block waiting for a reader that isn't ready yet.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original `ch` is unbuffered, so `ch <- count` can only complete at the exact moment some other goroutine is simultaneously executing `<-ch`. While main sleeps for 3 seconds the first send stays blocked, so the goroutine never gets past its first iteration. Here main's read eventually frees it; a caller that never reads would leave it stuck forever. The fix gives `ch` a buffer of 1 (`make(chan int, 1)`), so one send can complete and sit in the channel's buffer without any reader present, letting the sending goroutine keep making progress instead of blocking on every send. The `select`/`default` combination goes a step further and makes the send non-blocking: if the buffer already holds an unread heartbeat, the goroutine drops the new one instead of piling up or blocking, which matches the stated intent. (Both versions print `first heartbeat: 1`: the buffer holds the oldest unread value. The difference is whether the sender kept running. To let the goroutine stop altogether, you would also give it a done channel or a context.)

assessments.prompt: Why are goroutines described as 'lightweight' compared to OS threads?
options: Goroutines don't actually run real code concurrently -- they're simulated sequentially by the runtime, so there's no real scheduling overhead at all.
Goroutines are lightweight because Go silently limits every program to a maximum of a few dozen goroutines at once, keeping total resource usage low.
Goroutines start with a small (around 2KB), dynamically-growable stack and are scheduled by the Go runtime onto a small number of OS threads.
Goroutines use less memory because they cannot access any heap-allocated data, only their own local stack variables.
assessments.explanation: The resource difference is stack size and who does the scheduling: a goroutine's stack starts tiny (~2KB) and grows/shrinks dynamically as needed, while a typical OS thread reserves a large, fixed-size stack upfront regardless of actual need. Combined with the Go runtime multiplexing many goroutines onto a much smaller number of real OS threads (an M:N scheduler), this is what makes spinning up thousands of goroutines cheap where spinning up thousands of OS threads would not be. The “Goroutines don't actually run real code concurrently…” option is wrong: goroutines do run concurrently (and in parallel across multiple cores when GOMAXPROCS > 1), it's not a sequential simulation. The “Goroutines are lightweight because Go silently limits…” option is wrong: there's no such fixed cap; production Go programs routinely run into the hundreds of thousands of goroutines. The “Goroutines use less memory because they cannot…” option is wrong: goroutines can access heap-allocated data like any other Go code; that's unrelated to why they're lightweight.

assessments.prompt: A developer says: 'My Go program is running on an 8-core machine, so launching 8 goroutines guarantees all 8 run in true parallel, at the exact same instant.' What's the flaw in this claim?
options: Nothing is wrong with it -- Go always runs exactly as many goroutines in parallel as there are available cores.
True parallelism in Go requires manually pinning each goroutine to a specific CPU core through a dedicated API call.
Goroutines can never run in parallel under any circumstances; Go only ever provides the illusion of simultaneity through fast interleaving on a single core, regardless of core count.

Starting a goroutine with `go` guarantees concurrent structure (independent, interleavable progress), but whether execution actually becomes parallel -- multiple goroutines running at the exact same physical instant on separate cores -- depends on GOMAXPROCS and runtime scheduling decisions, not merely on how many goroutines you happened to start.
assessments.explanation: Concurrency is about structuring a program as independently-progressing pieces; parallelism is about whether hardware executes more than one of them at the same physical instant. The `go` keyword guarantees the former, but the runtime, guided by GOMAXPROCS and scheduling decisions, determines how much of that structure is run in parallel; launching 8 goroutines on an 8-core machine doesn't force the scheduler to run all 8 simultaneously at every instant. The “Nothing is wrong with it -- Go…” option overstates the guarantee. The number of cores available doesn't force that much simultaneous execution at all times. The “Goroutines can never run in parallel under…” option is wrong in the opposite direction. Go absolutely can and does run goroutines in true parallel when GOMAXPROCS > 1 and multiple goroutines are runnable. The “True parallelism in Go requires manually pinning…” option is wrong: there's no such manual core-pinning requirement in ordinary Go programming; the runtime handles this itself.

assessments.prompt:
What does this program most likely print?

```go
func main() {
	go fmt.Println("background work")
	fmt.Println("main done")
}
```
options: Both lines always print, in the order shown, because Go guarantees main finishes running its own remaining statements before any other queued goroutine gets a turn.
Just "main done" is by far the most likely single output, because main typically reaches its end -- and the whole process exits immediately when it does.
Only "background work" prints, because starting a goroutine with `go` pauses main until that goroutine finishes.
The program deadlocks, since main is not allowed to return while another goroutine is still queued to run.
assessments.explanation: When main returns, the entire program exits immediately, regardless of whether any other goroutines are still running or haven't started yet. Go does not wait for background goroutines on its own. Since `go fmt.Println(...)` returns control to the next line instantly without waiting for the goroutine to execute, main typically reaches its own end and triggers process exit before the scheduler gets around to running the new goroutine at all, so "main done" prints and "background work" usually never does. The “Both lines always print, in the order…” option is wrong: there's no such execution-order guarantee. The “The program deadlocks, since main…” option is wrong: Go never blocks main's return on other goroutines finishing; it returns immediately and the process exits. The “Only "background work" prints, because starting…” option is wrong: `go` never pauses the calling goroutine; it returns control immediately.

options: Most likely 3, 3, 3 (in some interleaving), because before Go 1.22 there was only one shared loop variable `i` reused across every iteration, so every goroutine's closure captured that same variable, which had typically already reached its final value of 3 by the time any goroutine actually got around to reading it.
Exactly 0, 1, 2, but merged into a single combined print statement, since all three goroutines share one underlying variable.
A compile error, because a closure can never reference a variable declared in a for loop's init clause, in any version of Go.
Reliably 0, 1, 2, in that exact order, since each goroutine's closure captures the loop variable's value at the moment that goroutine was launched.
assessments.explanation: Before Go 1.22, a `for` loop had exactly one instance of its loop variable for the entire loop, not a fresh one per iteration, so a closure created inside the loop body that references `i` captures that single shared variable, not a snapshot of its value at that moment. By the time any of the three goroutines runs, the loop has very likely already finished all three iterations, leaving `i` at 3, which is what every goroutine ends up printing. (The goroutines' reads also race with the loop's `i++`, so other results are possible.) The “Reliably 0, 1, 2, in that exact…” option describes neither version: Go 1.22+ gives each goroutine its own value, but no version guarantees the order they print in. The “A compile error, because a closure can…” option is wrong: referencing a loop variable from a closure is completely legal Go, in every version; it's the semantics of what gets captured that changed. The “Exactly 0, 1, 2, but merged into…” option is wrong: there's no merging of prints; each goroutine calls Println independently, they just each observe the same final value.

assessments.prompt: Explain what a goroutine leak is, why the garbage collector can't fix it, and what kind of code pattern typically causes one.
assessments.modelAnswer: A goroutine leak is a goroutine that becomes permanently blocked (almost always on a channel send or receive, or occasionally a lock, that will never be satisfied) and therefore never terminates for the rest of the program's lifetime. This differs fundamentally from a memory leak caused by holding an unnecessary reference to an object: Go's garbage collector reclaims memory for objects that are no longer reachable by any live part of the program, but a leaked goroutine is not unreachable garbage from the runtime's point of view. It's parked, waiting on an event that will never arrive, and the collector treats its stack as a root. It is never eligible for garbage collection, no matter how long it sits blocked; it continues to consume its stack memory and hold onto any resources or references it captured, for as long as the process keeps running. The most common cause is a mismatch between a goroutine's channel operation and its counterpart: a goroutine trying to send on an unbuffered (or full) channel that nothing will ever read from again, typically because the receiving code path already returned early (due to an error, a timeout, or a cancelled request) without ever getting to the point where it reads from that channel. In a long-running server, this kind of leak compounds: every request that hits the buggy code path leaks one more permanently-blocked goroutine, and over time this can exhaust memory even though no individual leak looks dramatic on its own. The general defense is designing every goroutine with an explicit way to be released even on the not-so-happy paths (via a context.Context that can be cancelled, a channel buffered generously enough that a send can't block, or a select statement offering an alternative path out) rather than assuming the 'normal' completion path is the only one that will ever execute.

assessments.prompt: A Go service spawns a goroutine per incoming request to call a slow downstream API. Under load, memory keeps growing until the pod is killed. What is likely happening and how would you fix it?
assessments.modelAnswer: Goroutines are cheap but not free, and each blocked one holds its stack and any buffers it references. If the downstream call has no timeout, or the goroutine writes to a channel nobody reads after the request returns, goroutines pile up forever: a goroutine leak. Confirm with the pprof goroutine profile or runtime.NumGoroutine over time. Fix by passing the request's context.Context to the downstream call and using http.Client with a timeout so work stops when the client disconnects or the deadline passes. Make channels buffered or use select with ctx.Done() so senders never block forever. Limit concurrency with a worker pool or a semaphore (a buffered channel or errgroup.SetLimit) so a traffic spike cannot create unbounded goroutines, and add a test using goleak to catch regressions.

concepts.title: Channels and select
concepts.description: Channels are Go's built-in mechanism for goroutines to communicate and synchronize by passing values, and select lets a goroutine wait on multiple channel operations at once: together they implement Go's famous slogan, "don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating."
learningObjectives: Create and use both unbuffered and buffered channels, and explain the blocking behavior difference between them.
Close a channel with `close` and explain what happens when receiving from a closed channel, including the two-value receive form.
Use `select` to wait on multiple channel operations simultaneously, including a `default` case for non-blocking behavior.
Explain the deadlock that results from sending on (or receiving from) a channel with no corresponding goroutine on the other end.
Use a channel as a signal (e.g. `done chan struct{}`) rather than as a value-carrying pipe.

sections.heading: Channels: Typed Pipes Between Goroutines
sections.body:
A **channel** is a typed conduit that one goroutine can send values into and another can receive values from, created with `make(chan T)` for some type `T`:

```go
ch := make(chan int)

go func() {
	ch <- 42        // send: blocks until another goroutine receives
}()

value := <-ch     // receive: blocks until another goroutine sends
fmt.Println(value)   // 42
```

By default, a channel created with `make(chan int)` is **unbuffered**: a send (`ch <- value`) blocks the sending goroutine until some other goroutine performs a matching receive (`<-ch`), and symmetrically, a receive blocks until a send is ready. An unbuffered channel operation is a rendezvous: when it completes, you know both sides were there. That is how channels coordinate goroutines as well as carry data.

`make(chan int, 3)` creates a **buffered** channel with room for 3 values in flight. A send into a buffered channel that isn't full completes immediately, without waiting for a receiver, only once the buffer is completely full does a further send block, waiting for some receive to make room. Buffering changes *when* blocking happens, but doesn't eliminate the possibility of blocking altogether; it's a tool for decoupling producer and consumer timing to a bounded degree, not a way to guarantee a send never waits.

sections.heading: Closing a Channel and the Two-Value Receive
sections.body:
`close(ch)` signals that no more values will ever be sent on a channel. It's a one-way, one-time announcement from whoever owns the sending side (as a strong convention: **only the sender should ever close a channel**, never the receiver, since closing a channel that might still receive further sends elsewhere is a recipe for a panic). Receiving from a closed channel never blocks: it first delivers any values still in the buffer, and after that every receive immediately returns the element type's zero value.

This creates an ambiguity a plain receive can't resolve on its own: did I get `0` because someone sent `0`, or because the channel is closed and has nothing left? The **two-value receive form** answers this:

```go
value, ok := <-ch
// ok is true if value was an actual sent value
// ok is false if the channel is closed and drained -- value is the zero value
```

`for value := range ch` is the idiomatic way to drain a channel until it's closed: it automatically receives repeatedly and exits the loop cleanly the moment the channel is closed and empty, without you needing to check `ok` by hand on every iteration. One more sharp edge: **sending on an already-closed channel panics immediately**, and **closing an already-closed channel also panics**: `close` is emphatically not idempotent, and there is no natural way to check 'is this channel already closed?' before closing it (checking via a receive would itself consume a value or race with other receivers). So give each channel one clear owner, who closes it once, and only after being certain no further sends will be attempted.

sections.heading: select: Waiting on Multiple Channels at Once
sections.body:
A single channel receive (`<-ch`) can only wait on one channel. `select` lets a goroutine wait on *several* channel operations simultaneously, proceeding with whichever one becomes ready first:

```go
select {
case msg := <-ch1:
	fmt.Println("from ch1:", msg)
case msg := <-ch2:
	fmt.Println("from ch2:", msg)
case <-time.After(2 * time.Second):
	fmt.Println("timed out waiting for either channel")
}
```

If more than one case is ready simultaneously, `select` picks one **at random** among the ready cases (not top-to-bottom, not by any priority), a design choice that stops code from accidentally depending on case ordering and forces each case to stand on its own. `time.After(d)` is an extremely common idiom seen inside a `select`: it returns a channel that receives a single value after duration `d` has elapsed, letting you implement a timeout for 'wait for this channel, but give up after N seconds' within the `select` itself, with no separate timer bookkeeping required.

Adding a `default` case makes the entire `select` **non-blocking**: if no other case is immediately ready, `default` runs right away instead of waiting for any of them. This is the standard way to attempt a send or receive 'if possible, otherwise move on': the pattern used to make a channel send non-blocking when you'd rather drop a value than stall (as in the previous concept's heartbeat exercise). A related fact: a send or receive on a nil channel blocks forever, so setting a channel variable to `nil` switches off its case inside a `select` loop.

sections.heading: Deadlock: Nobody Left to Meet the Rendezvous
Channels as Signals, Not Just Pipes
sections.body:
Not every channel exists to carry meaningful data: a very common Go idiom uses a channel purely as a **signal**, where the fact that a receive succeeded (or that the channel was closed) is the entire message, and the value itself is irrelevant. `chan struct{}` is the idiomatic type for this: `struct{}` is the empty struct, which occupies zero bytes of memory, making it the natural 'I don't care about the payload, only the event' type.

```go
done := make(chan struct{})

go func() {
	doWork()
	close(done)   // signal: "I'm finished" -- the value never mattered, only the closing
}()

<-done   // blocks until doWork() has finished and done is closed
fmt.Println("worker finished")
```

Closing `done` (rather than sending a value into it) is the usual choice here because closing broadcasts to *every* current and future receiver simultaneously and forever. If multiple goroutines are all waiting on `<-done`, closing it releases all of them at once, whereas a single sent value would only satisfy one waiting receiver. This exact pattern (an unbuffered or closed `chan struct{}` used purely as a completion/cancellation signal) is also the conceptual seed of `context.Context`'s cancellation mechanism, which you'll encounter in later, more advanced material; internally, a cancelled context is implemented by closing this kind of signal channel.

examples.title: Unbuffered vs. Buffered Send Blocking Behavior
examples.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	unbuffered := make(chan int)
	buffered := make(chan int, 2)

	buffered <- 1   // succeeds immediately -- buffer has room
	buffered <- 2   // succeeds immediately -- buffer now full (2/2)
	fmt.Println("both buffered sends completed without any receiver")

	go func() {
		fmt.Println(<-unbuffered)   // the receiver that makes the next line possible
	}()
	unbuffered <- 42   // blocks until the goroutine above is ready to receive
	fmt.Println("unbuffered send completed once a receiver showed up")
}
examples.explanation: The two sends into `buffered` both complete instantly with no receiver anywhere in sight, because the channel's buffer (capacity 2) has room for both values: buffering lets a send succeed without a rendezvous, up to that capacity. `unbuffered`, by contrast, has zero buffer capacity, so `unbuffered <- 42` cannot proceed until some other goroutine is simultaneously ready to receive; that's why the receiving goroutine is launched first, on the line above, so it's available to complete the rendezvous the moment the main goroutine's send is attempted. Without that goroutine existing at all, `unbuffered <- 42` in `main`, the only goroutine, would deadlock the entire program, as shown in the deadlock section above. (The program may exit before the goroutine gets to print 42; nothing makes main wait for that Println.)

examples.title: select With a Timeout via time.After
examples.explanation: `slowOperation` takes 3 seconds before it can send on `result`, but the `select` is only willing to wait 1 second, via the channel `time.After(1 * time.Second)` returns: that channel receives exactly one value once its duration elapses, and nothing before that. Because the timeout case becomes ready well before `result` ever will, `select` picks the timeout branch and prints "gave up waiting after 1 second"; the still-running `slowOperation` goroutine eventually finishes its sleep and tries to send on `result` regardless, at which point (with no receiver left, since main's select already moved on and main will likely exit soon after) it may itself become a leaked goroutine if nothing ever drains `result`. A timeout in a `select` frees the goroutine doing the selecting; it does nothing for the abandoned goroutine on the other end. Making `result` a channel with a buffer of 1 would let that goroutine send and exit.

examples.title: Broadcasting Completion With a Closed Signal Channel
examples.explanation: All three worker goroutines block on `<-done` at roughly the same time, each waiting for the signal channel to produce something. `close(done)` is what releases them, and it releases *all three at once*, not just one, because a closed channel returns its zero value immediately and repeatedly to every current and future receiver, forever. If `done <- struct{}{}` had been used instead of closing (sending one signal value rather than closing the channel), only one of the three waiting goroutines would receive that single value; the other two would remain blocked indefinitely, since nothing else would ever be sent. This is why 'close to broadcast a completion signal to everyone waiting' is the idiomatic pattern when multiple goroutines need to be released by the same event, rather than sending distinct values to each one individually.

misconceptions.description: Sending a value into a buffered channel, like `make(chan int, 5)`, never blocks -- that's the whole point of giving it a buffer.
misconceptions.clarification: A buffered channel only avoids blocking on a send while the buffer has free capacity. Once the buffer is completely full (all 5 slots occupied by unreceived values, in this example), the very next send blocks like an unbuffered channel would, waiting until some goroutine performs a receive to free up a slot. Buffering shifts *when* blocking kicks in (after N values are already in flight, rather than immediately), and can smooth over short bursts of timing mismatch between producer and consumer, but it does not remove the possibility of blocking altogether for a producer that's consistently faster than its consumer.
misconceptions.fact: A buffered channel only avoids blocking on a send while the buffer has free capacity.

misconceptions.description: If several goroutines are all blocked waiting to receive from a channel, and one goroutine sends a single value, all of the waiting goroutines receive a copy of that value.
misconceptions.clarification: A single sent value satisfies exactly one waiting receiver. Go channels are point-to-point for actual sent values, not a broadcast mechanism; the runtime picks one of the waiting receivers to hand that value to, and the rest remain blocked, still waiting. Broadcasting to every current and future waiter simultaneously requires closing the channel instead of sending a value. A closed channel returns its zero value to every receive, present and future, which is the mechanism used for 'release everyone waiting on this signal at once,' as opposed to 'hand this one specific value to whichever one receiver happens to be selected.'
misconceptions.fact: A single sent value satisfies exactly one waiting receiver. Go channels are point-to-point for actual sent values, not a broadcast mechanism; the runtime picks one of the waiting receivers to hand that value to, and the rest remain blocked, still waiting.

exercises.prompt: What happens when this program runs?
hints: The channel is buffered with room for 2, and exactly 2 values are sent before it's closed. Both sends should succeed without needing a receiver present yet.
`for v := range ch` keeps receiving until the channel is BOTH closed AND drained of any remaining buffered values: closing alone doesn't discard values still sitting in the buffer.
Think about whether closing a channel that still has buffered values in it prevents those values from being received afterward.
exercises.expectedAnswer: It prints 1, then 2, then "loop finished cleanly", with no panic and no deadlock. Closing a channel doesn't discard values already sitting in its buffer; range continues to receive those remaining buffered values first, and only exits once the channel is both closed and fully drained.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Both `ch <- 1` and `ch <- 2` succeed immediately with no receiver present, because the channel's buffer has capacity 2 and neither send exceeds it. `close(ch)` marks the channel as closed for any further sends, but it does not erase or invalidate the two values already sitting in the buffer: `for v := range ch` continues to receive them in order (1, then 2) as if the channel were still open, and only exits the loop once the buffer is empty and the channel is closed, which the range loop detects automatically without you needing to check the two-value `ok` form by hand. The final print then runs normally, since nothing here panics or blocks forever: closing a channel that still has buffered values is completely legitimate and a common pattern for 'no more values are coming, but drain whatever's left first.'

exercises.prompt: This program is supposed to collect results from 3 worker goroutines into a slice and print them, but it never prints: it dies with 'fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!'. Find and fix the bug.
hints: `for v := range results` only stops once `results` is closed. Does anything in this program ever call close(results)?
Each worker sends exactly once and then returns: nobody is left with a responsibility to close the channel once all 3 sends have happened.

You need some way to know when all 3 workers are done, so you can close the channel exactly once, after all sends: consider a sync.WaitGroup combined with a separate goroutine that waits on it and then closes the channel.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original code's `for v := range results` will only ever stop once `results` is closed, but nothing in the program ever calls `close(results)`: each worker sends its one value and returns, and nobody takes responsibility for closing the channel afterward, so after receiving 3 values `range` waits for a 4th that will never arrive. By then the workers have returned and main is the only goroutine left, so the runtime detects the deadlock and crashes the program. (In a larger program with other goroutines still running, the same bug would hang main with no error.) The fix adds a `sync.WaitGroup` so something can know when all 3 workers have finished sending, and a separate goroutine that calls `wg.Wait()` and then `close(results)`: closing exactly once, only after every worker's send has completed. That close is what lets the `range` loop in main correctly exit once all 3 values have been drained, and the program prints its result.

assessments.prompt: Why does Go's `select` statement pick randomly among multiple ready cases, rather than always choosing the first ready case in source-code order?
options: It only picks randomly when exactly two cases are ready; with three or more ready cases, it always picks the first one in source order.
Randomizing improves raw performance by letting the runtime skip checking later cases once an earlier one is found ready.
It's a deliberate design choice that prevents code from accidentally depending on the order cases happen to be written in.
It's an unavoidable limitation of how the Go runtime schedules goroutines, not a deliberate design choice.
assessments.explanation: Go's select statement is specified to choose uniformly at random among whichever cases are ready at the moment it evaluates them, so that developers can't accidentally write code that only works because case A happens to be listed before case B. Every case must be written as if it could be the one chosen, regardless of position. The “It's an unavoidable limitation of how…” option is wrong: this is a specified language behavior, not an incidental scheduling quirk. The “Randomizing improves raw performance by letting…” option is wrong and describes the opposite of what happens: picking randomly among all ready cases requires checking all of them, not stopping early. The “It only picks randomly when exactly two…” option is wrong: there's no special-casing based on the number of ready cases; the same random-choice rule applies uniformly regardless of how many cases happen to be ready.

assessments.prompt: Which of the following correctly describes close(ch) in Go?
options: Closing a channel automatically discards any values still sitting unread in its buffer, so a subsequent `range` over it receives nothing at all.
Sending on a channel after it has already been closed panics immediately, and closing an already-closed channel also panics -- close is not idempotent.
Either the sender or the receiver side may safely call close(ch) at any point, since which goroutine owns the channel has no bearing on who is allowed to close it.
Calling close(ch) a second time on the same channel is a harmless no-op, just like calling it once.
assessments.explanation: close is a sharp, one-time operation: sending on a closed channel panics immediately, and calling close a second time on the same channel also panics. There is no idempotent 'close if not already closed' built in, and checking beforehand via a receive would itself consume a value or race with other receivers. This is why the strong convention is a single, clear owner (the sender) responsible for closing exactly once. The “Closing a channel automatically discards any values…” option is wrong: values already sitting in a closed channel's buffer are still delivered; range continues draining them in order before it exits. The “Either the sender or the receiver side…” option is wrong: only the sending side should ever close a channel; a receiver closing it risks a panic on a subsequent send from the actual sender. The “Calling close(ch) a second time…” option is wrong: a second close() call panics, it does not silently no-op.

assessments.prompt:
In this code, what happens if neither ch1 nor ch2 has a value ready to receive at the exact moment the select statement runs?

```go
select {
case v := <-ch1:
	fmt.Println("ch1:", v)
case v := <-ch2:
	fmt.Println("ch2:", v)
default:
	fmt.Println("nothing ready")
}
```
options: This is a compile error, since a default case cannot be combined with channel-receive cases in the same select statement.
select blocks until either ch1 or ch2 becomes ready, ignoring the default case, since default only runs after some implicit timeout elapses.
select still picks randomly between ch1 and ch2 despite neither being ready, and blocks until whichever one it picked actually becomes ready.

The default case runs immediately -- adding a default case makes the entire select non-blocking, firing right away whenever no other case is immediately ready, instead of waiting for one to become ready.
assessments.explanation: Adding a default case is specifically what turns a select from blocking into non-blocking: if none of the other cases are ready the instant select evaluates them, default runs immediately instead of waiting for any of them to become ready. The “select blocks until either ch1 or ch2…” option inverts the actual behavior: default has nothing to do with timeouts; it fires immediately, not after a delay. The “This is a compile error, since…” option is wrong: combining default with receive/send cases in the same select is a completely standard, common pattern. The “select still picks randomly between ch1…” option is wrong: select only chooses randomly among cases that are ready; if none are, and a default exists, default is what runs, not a blocking random pick.

assessments.prompt: Three goroutines are all currently blocked on `<-done`, waiting for a completion signal. Which statement correctly describes how to release all three?
options: Closing the channel with `close(done)` releases all three simultaneously, because a closed channel returns its zero value immediately and repeatedly to every current and future receiver -- whereas sending a single value would satisfy only one of the three waiting receivers, leaving the other two blocked.
Sending one value with `done <- struct{}{}` releases all three simultaneously, since a channel send is automatically broadcast to every goroutine currently waiting to receive.
Neither sending nor closing can ever release more than one waiting goroutine; each of the three would need its own dedicated channel to be released at all.
Sending three separate values, one at a time, is required to release all three, and closing the channel would have no effect on any goroutine currently blocked on a receive.
assessments.explanation: A single sent value satisfies exactly one waiting receiver: Go channels hand a sent value to only one of the waiting goroutines, not all of them. Closing a channel, by contrast, is a broadcast: every current and future receive on that channel immediately returns the zero value, forever, which is why closing (rather than sending) is the idiomatic way to release every goroutine waiting on a shared signal at once. The “Sending one value with `done <- struct{}{}`…” option describes a broadcast-on-send behavior Go channels don't have. The “Neither sending nor closing can ever release…” option understates what closing accomplishes; one close does release all three. The “Sending three separate values, one…” option is wrong on both counts: three sends would indeed eventually satisfy three separate receivers one at a time, but closing very much does affect all currently-blocked receives, releasing them immediately.

assessments.prompt: Explain the difference between a full-program deadlock and a goroutine leak in Go, and why Go's runtime can detect and crash on one but not the other.
assessments.modelAnswer: Both involve a goroutine blocked forever on an operation, typically a channel send or receive, that will never be completed by anything else. The difference is scope: a full-program deadlock is the situation where every goroutine in the entire program is simultaneously blocked, with no goroutine anywhere left running that could possibly unblock any of the others. The whole program has come to a complete, permanent stop. Go's runtime actively monitors for this global condition, and when it detects that nothing is runnable anywhere, it crashes the program immediately with 'fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!' rather than hanging forever, so the bug surfaces at once during development. A goroutine leak, by contrast, is a partial condition: one or more goroutines are permanently stuck, but the rest of the program (including main, and possibly many other goroutines) keeps making ongoing progress. Because the program as a whole is not stuck, the runtime's deadlock detector has nothing to trigger on; from its point of view, things are fine, since at least one goroutine somewhere is still runnable. This is why leaks are more dangerous in practice than full deadlocks: a deadlock announces itself loudly and immediately during testing or even production, forcing a fix, while a leak can accumulate stuck goroutines one at a time (often triggered by a specific, maybe rare, error-handling code path) for hours or days in a long-running service, slowly consuming memory, until it eventually degrades or crashes the process with no clear, single, reproducible trigger to point at.

concepts.title: The sync Package: Mutex and WaitGroup
concepts.description: sync.Mutex protects shared state from concurrent access, and sync.WaitGroup lets one goroutine wait for a group of others to finish: the two most common tools for coordinating goroutines when a channel isn't the natural fit.
learningObjectives: Explain what a data race is and why concurrent unsynchronized access to shared memory is a program error in Go, not merely 'probably fine.'
Use sync.Mutex (Lock/Unlock) to protect a shared variable from concurrent access, including with defer.
Use sync.WaitGroup (Add/Done/Wait) to wait for a known number of goroutines to finish.
Explain why forgetting to call wg.Add before launching a goroutine (or calling it inside the goroutine) is a race condition in itself.
Run the race detector (`go run -race`) and explain what kind of bug it actually catches.

sections.heading: Data Races: Why Unsynchronized Shared Access Is a Bug
sections.body:
A **data race** occurs when two or more goroutines access the same memory location concurrently, at least one of those accesses is a write, and there's no synchronization ordering one access relative to the other. The Go memory model calls a data race an error and allows an implementation to report it and terminate the program. Go is stricter than C or C++, where a race is undefined behavior and anything may happen: in Go, a racing read of a value no larger than a machine word must return some value that was really written to that location. But it need not be the latest one, writes may appear to other goroutines in a surprising order, and a race on anything larger than a word (a string, a slice, an interface) can give you a torn value: the pointer from one write and the length from another. Using such a value can corrupt memory.

```go
counter := 0
var wg sync.WaitGroup
for i := 0; i < 1000; i++ {
	wg.Add(1)
	go func() {
		defer wg.Done()
		counter++   // DATA RACE: read-modify-write with no synchronization
	}()
}
wg.Wait()
fmt.Println(counter)   // may print less than 1000; the result varies from run to run
```

`counter++` is not a single atomic operation. It takes three steps: read the current value, add one, write it back. When two goroutines interleave those steps (goroutine A reads 5, goroutine B also reads 5 before A writes back, both compute 6, both write 6; one increment is lost), the final count can end up lower than 1000, and by how much varies from run to run. On a given machine the race may not fire every time, which is part of what makes it dangerous. The next two tools fix different halves of this kind of problem.

sections.heading: sync.Mutex: Mutual Exclusion
sections.body:
A **mutex** (mutual exclusion lock) ensures that only one goroutine at a time can execute the section of code between a `Lock()` and its matching `Unlock()`. Any other goroutine calling `Lock()` while it's already held blocks until the holder calls `Unlock()`. This turns the unsafe `counter++` above into something safe:

```go
var (
	counter int
	mu      sync.Mutex
)

func increment() {
	mu.Lock()
	defer mu.Unlock()
	counter++
}
```

`defer mu.Unlock()` immediately after `mu.Lock()` is close to a fixed idiom in Go, because it guarantees the unlock happens no matter how the function exits, including via an early `return`, or even a `panic` unwinding through the function. Without `defer`, a function with multiple return paths or the possibility of panicking would need to remember to call `Unlock()` on every one of those paths, and missing even one leaves the mutex permanently locked: every other goroutine that ever tries to `Lock()` it again blocks forever, effectively becoming a self-inflicted deadlock (or, more precisely, a goroutine leak affecting every future caller). Recall from the Structs and Methods concept that `sync.Mutex`'s zero value is already a valid, unlocked mutex: `var mu sync.Mutex` needs no constructor, which is why you'll see it declared as a plain struct field with no initialization step anywhere.

**A `sync.Mutex` (like most sync types) must never be copied after first use.** If a struct contains a `sync.Mutex` field, pass that struct around by pointer, not by value: copying it duplicates the lock's internal state, and the copy no longer protects the same critical section as the original, which defeats the point of having a mutex. `go vet` (its `copylocks` check) catches many of these mistakes, but not every one.

sections.heading: sync.WaitGroup: Waiting for a Known Number of Goroutines
sections.body:
`sync.WaitGroup` solves a different, extremely common problem: 'launch N goroutines, and don't proceed until all N have finished.' It has exactly three methods that matter: `Add(n)` increments an internal counter by `n`; `Done()` decrements it by 1 (and is equivalent to `Add(-1)`); `Wait()` blocks until that counter reaches zero.

```go
var wg sync.WaitGroup
for i := 0; i < 5; i++ {
	wg.Add(1)
	go func(id int) {
		defer wg.Done()
		fmt.Println("worker", id, "running")
	}(i)
}
wg.Wait()   // blocks until all 5 workers have called Done()
fmt.Println("all workers finished")
```

The placement of `wg.Add(1)` matters more than it might look like at first glance: it must happen in the goroutine that is *launching* the new goroutine, **before** the `go` statement, never inside the new goroutine itself. If `Add` were called inside the goroutine, there would be a race between that `Add` executing and the main goroutine reaching `wg.Wait()`: if `Wait()` runs before any goroutine gets around to calling its own `Add(1)`, the counter could still be at zero, and `Wait()` would return immediately, believing (incorrectly) that there's nothing left to wait for, even though goroutines are still queued up or newly starting. Calling `Add` in the launching goroutine, before `go`, guarantees the counter reflects every goroutine that's about to run before `Wait()` has any chance to check it.

`defer wg.Done()` at the very top of the goroutine's body mirrors the `defer mu.Unlock()` idiom for the same reason: it guarantees `Done()` fires no matter how that goroutine's body exits, including through an early return or a panic, and a missed `Done()` call means the counter never reaches zero, so `wg.Wait()` blocks forever, another way to leak a goroutine (this time the waiting one).

Go 1.25 added `wg.Go(f)`, which does the `Add(1)`, starts the goroutine, and calls `Done` when `f` returns: `wg.Go(func() { fmt.Println("worker", id, "running") })`. On 1.25 or later, prefer it, since it makes the misplaced-`Add` bug impossible. You will keep meeting `Add`/`Done` in existing code.

sections.heading: Mutex vs. Channel: Choosing the Right Tool
sections.body:
Go offers two coordination styles: channels (share memory by communicating) and the sync package (traditional locking). As a rough guideline, use a **mutex** when you have a piece of shared *state* (a counter, a cache, a map) that multiple goroutines need to read and mutate directly, and the natural unit of work is 'briefly touch this shared data structure and move on.' Use a **channel** when you're coordinating the *flow* of values or signals between goroutines (handing off work items, fanning results back in, signaling completion or cancellation) where the interesting thing is the handoff itself, not a piece of state sitting still that many goroutines poke at.

These aren't mutually exclusive, and idiomatic Go code frequently uses both together: a worker pool might use channels to distribute jobs and collect results, while a mutex-protected map inside one of those workers tracks some running statistic. Neither is more idiomatic than the other; a channel wrapped around a plain counter is usually slower and harder to read than a mutex.

sections.heading: The Race Detector: A Tool, Not a Guess
sections.body:
Data races are notoriously hard to catch by running a program and looking at its output, because a race might only manifest under specific timing that doesn't reliably occur on your machine, in your test run, today. Go ships with a built-in **race detector**, enabled with the `-race` flag on `go run`, `go build`, or `go test`: `go run -race main.go`. It instruments memory accesses at runtime and watches for unsynchronized concurrent access to the same memory location, reporting the exact goroutines, stack traces, and memory addresses involved the moment it observes one, rather than requiring you to somehow spot a wrong final number and reverse-engineer where the race must be coming from.

`-race` can only detect races that **occur during that specific run**. If the particular interleaving that triggers a race doesn't happen to occur while the instrumented program is running (because the buggy code path wasn't exercised, or the timing didn't line up that time), `-race` reports nothing, even though the race is still latent in the code and could surface on a different run, a different machine, or under different load. A clean `-race` run is evidence, not proof. Many teams run their test suite with `-race` in CI. They rarely ship `-race` binaries, because the Go documentation puts the typical cost at 5-10x the memory and 2-20x the execution time.

examples.title: The Unsynchronized Counter Race, and the Mutex Fix
examples.explanation: Every one of the 1000 goroutines now acquires `mu` before touching `counter`, and releases it immediately afterward via `defer mu.Unlock()`, so the read-increment-write sequence inside `counter++` can never be interrupted by another goroutine partway through; whichever goroutine holds the lock completes its full read-modify-write cycle before any other goroutine's `Lock()` call is allowed to proceed. This is the difference between the earlier unsynchronized version (which can under-count by a different amount each run, due to lost updates from interleaved reads and writes) and this version, which reliably prints exactly 1000 on every run, because the mutex has eliminated the possibility of that interleaving. `wg.Add(1)` before each `go func()` and `defer wg.Done()` as the first line of each goroutine together guarantee `wg.Wait()` doesn't return until all 1000 goroutines have finished incrementing.

examples.title: The wg.Add Placement Bug
examples.explanation: `wg.Add(1)` is called from inside each newly-launched goroutine rather than by the loop, before `go func(id int) {...}(i)` starts it. This creates a race between the main goroutine reaching `wg.Wait()` and each launched goroutine getting scheduled and executing its own `wg.Add(1)`. If `Wait()` happens to run before any goroutine has called `Add`, the WaitGroup's internal counter is still 0, and `Wait()` returns immediately, believing there's nothing to wait for, even though 5 goroutines are about to run (or are mid-flight) and will append to `results` afterward. The result is that `len(results)` printed by main is unreliable: it might occasionally be 5 if scheduling happens to work out, but frequently prints fewer, and the exact number varies unpredictably run to run. The fix is always to call `wg.Add(1)` in the loop itself, immediately before each `go` statement, so the counter correctly reflects every goroutine about to be launched before `Wait()` ever has a chance to check it.

examples.title: Passing a Mutex-Containing Struct by Pointer, Not Value
examples.explanation: `counter` is a `*SafeCounter` (a pointer), created with `&SafeCounter{}`, and every one of the 100 goroutines calls `Increment()` on that same underlying struct through that same pointer, so all 100 calls are contending for, and correctly synchronized by, the exact same `mu`. This matters because `sync.Mutex` must never be copied after use: if `Increment` had a value receiver (`func (c SafeCounter) Increment()`), each call would receive its own independent copy of the entire struct, including a copy of `mu`, meaning every goroutine would be locking and unlocking its own private, freshly-copied mutex that has nothing to do with any other goroutine's copy, providing zero actual protection for the shared `count` field (which, being copied too, wouldn't even be the field other goroutines see anyway). The pointer receiver is what makes this whole pattern correct: every goroutine reaches the same struct, the same mutex, and the same count field, rather than each getting its own disconnected copy.

misconceptions.description: A data race in Go just means you might occasionally read a slightly outdated value -- annoying, but generally harmless, similar to eventual consistency in a distributed system.
misconceptions.clarification: A data race is an error in the Go memory model, not merely a staleness issue. For values up to a machine word, a racing read returns some value that was written, but with no promise about which one or about the order in which other goroutines see writes, and concurrent read-modify-write sequences lose updates. For larger values (strings, slices, interfaces), a race can produce a torn value that no goroutine ever wrote, such as one string's pointer with another string's length, and using it can crash the program or corrupt memory. None of that resembles eventual consistency, where the value eventually settles on something somebody wrote.
misconceptions.fact: A data race is an error in the Go memory model, not merely a staleness issue.

misconceptions.description: It doesn't matter whether `wg.Add(1)` is called just before launching a goroutine or as the first line inside that goroutine -- either way, the counter gets incremented before the goroutine finishes, so wg.Wait() will work correctly.
misconceptions.clarification: It matters a great deal, because of when `wg.Wait()` might be called relative to when the goroutine gets scheduled and starts running. If `Add(1)` is called inside the goroutine rather than by the launching code before `go`, there's a window where the goroutine has been started but hasn't yet run far enough to call its own `Add(1)`, and if the launching goroutine reaches `wg.Wait()` during that window, it sees a counter that hasn't been incremented yet, may already be zero, and returns immediately, incorrectly believing there's nothing left to wait for. Calling `Add(1)` in the launching code, immediately before the `go` statement, guarantees the counter reflects that goroutine's existence before `Wait()` could possibly be reached, eliminating that race.

exercises.prompt: Will this program reliably print 500 every time it's run? Explain why or why not.
hints: wg.Add/Done/Wait correctly ensures main waits for all 500 goroutines to finish, but does that alone protect `total` itself from concurrent access?
`total++` is a read-modify-write operation involving 3 separate steps, not one atomic step. What happens if two goroutines' steps interleave?
sync.WaitGroup solves the 'wait for completion' problem; it does nothing at all to protect shared data from being read and written concurrently. That's a separate concern requiring a separate tool.
exercises.expectedAnswer: No. It can print something less than 500, and the number can vary from run to run (a lucky run may still print 500). wg correctly waits for all 500 goroutines to finish, but total++ is a data race: nothing synchronizes access to `total` itself, so concurrent read-modify-write interleavings across goroutines cause some increments to be silently lost.
exercises.solutionExplanation: sync.WaitGroup only tracks and signals completion. It guarantees wg.Wait() doesn't return until all 500 goroutines have called wg.Done(), but it provides zero protection for any shared data those goroutines touch along the way. `total++` expands to a read, an addition, and a write, and with no mutex or other synchronization guarding `total`, two goroutines can interleave those steps: both read the same current value, both independently compute value+1, and both write back the same result, losing one of the two increments. Across 500 goroutines racing like this, some number of increments get lost this way, so the final total can end up below 500, and because the exact interleaving depends on unpredictable scheduling, the specific shortfall varies from run to run rather than being a fixed, reproducible number. Fixing this requires wrapping `total++` in a sync.Mutex Lock/Unlock (or using sync/atomic for a simple counter like this), separate from the WaitGroup, which is solving a different problem.

exercises.prompt: This code is meant to safely record scores from multiple goroutines into a shared map, but it has a data race and on some runs crashes with 'fatal error: concurrent map writes'. Find and fix the bug.
hints: Go's built-in map type is explicitly documented as NOT safe for concurrent use without extra synchronization: multiple goroutines writing to the same map at the same time can crash the whole program, not just lose data.
sync.WaitGroup here correctly waits for all 5 goroutines to finish, but does nothing to serialize their access to the shared `scores` map while they're running.
Add a sync.Mutex, and Lock it around each goroutine's access to the map: Lock immediately before the map write, Unlock (ideally via defer) immediately after.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Go's built-in map type is not safe for concurrent access. The runtime makes a best-effort check for concurrent writes (and concurrent read/write mixes) to the same map and, when it notices one, stops the program with a fatal error that `recover` cannot catch. With only 5 short goroutines it may go unnoticed on most runs; `go run -race` reports it reliably. `sync.WaitGroup` in the original code correctly ensures main waits for all 5 goroutines to finish, but it does absolutely nothing to prevent those 5 goroutines from writing into `scores` at the same moment as each other, which is what triggers the crash. The fix introduces a `sync.Mutex`, locked immediately before each goroutine's map write and unlocked (via `defer`) immediately after: this serializes access to `scores` so that only one goroutine is ever writing into the map at any given instant, so there is no concurrent access left to detect.

assessments.prompt: A team lead says: 'We ran the program under `go run -race` for an hour and it reported nothing, so I'm confident this code has no data races anywhere.' What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options: The -race flag only checks for races in the first few seconds of program execution, then stops monitoring to save overhead.

The race detector can only report races that actually occur during the instrumented run -- if a particular buggy interleaving or code path wasn't exercised during that hour, it produces no warning, even though the race may still be latent in the code.
go run -race doesn't actually detect data races at all -- it only detects full-program deadlocks.
The race detector only works on code that uses channels, not sync.Mutex, so it wouldn't have caught mutex-related races anyway.
assessments.explanation: The race detector instruments actual memory accesses during a real execution and reports races it observes, but it cannot report a race whose triggering interleaving or code path didn't happen to occur during that specific run. A clean hour-long run is meaningful evidence that no race was triggered under that particular load and timing, not a proof that the code is race-free under all possible timings, inputs, and schedules. The “The race detector only works on code…” option is wrong: the race detector works on any memory access, including those protected (or unprotected) by sync.Mutex, not just channel operations. The “The -race flag only checks for races…” option is wrong: there's no such time-limited monitoring window; it runs for the duration of the instrumented program. The “go run -race doesn't actually detect data…” option is wrong: data race detection is what -race is for; full deadlock detection is a separate, always-on runtime feature that doesn't require the -race flag at all.

assessments.prompt: A developer claims: 'A data race just means a goroutine might read a slightly stale value -- annoying, but basically harmless, similar to eventual consistency in a distributed system.' What's wrong with this claim, according to how the Go memory model treats a data race?
options: Nothing is wrong with it -- that's an accurate description of what a data race causes in Go.
A data race only ever affects program performance, slowing execution down, but it can never affect the correctness of any value that gets read.
A data race is a program error: updates can be lost, and a racing read of a multiword value can return a torn value nobody wrote.
Data races are actually impossible in Go, since the runtime automatically serializes every memory access across goroutines behind the scenes.
assessments.explanation: Go's memory model treats a race as an error that an implementation may report by terminating the program. Word-sized reads return some value that was written (Go is stricter than C and C++ here), but concurrent increments still lose updates, and a race on anything larger than a machine word, such as a string or an interface, can produce a value assembled from two different writes. The “Data races are actually impossible in Go…” option is wrong: Go does not automatically serialize unsynchronized accesses; that's why races are possible and dangerous. The “A data race only ever affects program…” option is wrong: races are fundamentally a correctness problem, not merely a performance one.

assessments.prompt: A struct contains a sync.Mutex field. Which statement correctly describes how values of this struct should be handled once that mutex has been used?
options: sync.Mutex is a reference type under the hood, similar to a slice or a map, so copying a struct that contains one never actually duplicates the lock.
go vet is guaranteed to catch every single case of a copied mutex, so this isn't something a developer needs to reason about manually.
It's always safe to copy such a struct freely, at any point, since Go automatically shares the underlying lock state across every copy of the same original value.
The struct should always be passed around and referenced via a pointer from that point on -- copying it duplicates the mutex's internal state.
assessments.explanation: sync.Mutex (like most types in the sync package) must never be copied after first use. Copying duplicates its internal state, producing an independent lock that has nothing to do with the original: goroutines locking the copy provide zero protection for whatever the original mutex was guarding. The practical rule is to pass such a struct by pointer once it's in use. The “It's always safe to copy such…” and “sync.Mutex is a reference type under…” options both wrongly assume some kind of automatic sharing or reference semantics that sync.Mutex does not have. It's an ordinary struct value like any other, which is why copying it is dangerous. The “go vet is guaranteed to catch every…” option overstates go vet's coverage: its copylocks check catches many cases of this mistake but not all of them.

assessments.prompt: Based on the rough guideline for choosing between a mutex and a channel, which scenario is the more natural fit for a sync.Mutex rather than a channel?
options: Multiple goroutines that each need to briefly read and update a shared in-memory cache map before moving on to their own separate work.
Signaling every currently-waiting goroutine at once that a long-running setup step has finished, so they can all proceed simultaneously.
One goroutine producing a stream of computed values that another goroutine consumes one at a time, in order.
A worker pool that hands off individual job items to several workers, then collects each worker's result back through another channel.
assessments.explanation: The guideline favors a mutex when there's a piece of shared state that multiple goroutines need to directly read and mutate, with the natural unit of work being 'briefly touch this shared data structure and move on': what a shared cache map being read and updated by multiple goroutines looks like. The other three scenarios are all shaped around the flow of values or signals between goroutines rather than a piece of state sitting still being poked at: handing off job items and collecting results is a channel-shaped handoff, broadcasting a one-time completion signal to many waiters is the closed-channel broadcast pattern, and a producer/consumer stream processed in order is what an ordinary channel pipe is for.

assessments.prompt: Explain why sync.WaitGroup and sync.Mutex solve two different problems, using an example where a program might correctly use one but still be buggy without the other.
assessments.modelAnswer: sync.WaitGroup solves a completion-tracking problem: it lets one goroutine know when a specific, known number of other goroutines have all finished running, via Add to register expected work, Done to mark one unit of work complete, and Wait to block until the count returns to zero. It says nothing whatsoever about what those goroutines do to shared data while they're running, or whether their accesses to that data are safe relative to each other. It purely tracks 'how many are still in flight.' sync.Mutex solves a completely different problem: mutual exclusion, ensuring that only one goroutine at a time can execute a particular section of code (typically a section that reads or writes some piece of shared state) so that concurrent accesses can't interleave in a way that corrupts or loses data. A concrete example that uses WaitGroup correctly but is still buggy without a Mutex: spinning up 1000 goroutines that each increment a shared `int` counter, wrapped correctly with wg.Add(1) before each launch and defer wg.Done() inside each goroutine, then calling wg.Wait() in main. The WaitGroup usage is correct here: main really will wait until all 1000 goroutines have finished running before it proceeds. But without a mutex (or an equivalent, like sync/atomic) protecting the counter's read-modify-write increment, those 1000 goroutines can still race on the counter itself, causing some increments to be lost due to interleaved reads and writes, so the final printed count frequently comes out below 1000, varying by run. The program 'waits correctly' thanks to WaitGroup while simultaneously producing a wrong answer due to the missing Mutex. One tool answers 'has everyone finished,' the other answers 'is it safe for everyone to touch this data at once,' and a program can get either one right while still getting the other wrong.
